Monday night through Tuesday: An upper-level ridge shifts into 
the Inland Northwest tonight ahead of an approaching frontal 
system. Abundant boundary layer moisture from Sunday’s 
precipitation, combined with light winds, will maintain areas of
stratus and fog across the region. A warm front lifts northward
across western and central Washington tonight. While meridional
flow aloft focuses the primary moisture plume west of the 
Cascade crest, and model guidance continues to show spread 
regarding the eastward extent of precipitation, low-level 
southeasterly upslope flow will focus the best precipitation 
chances along the Cascade crest and east slopes.

Snow accumulations of 1 to 4 inches are forecast for Stevens 
Pass, the upper Wenatchee River Valley (including Leavenworth 
and Plain), and the Methow Valley, where residual cold air 
remains trapped. Surface observations in Leavenworth currently 
show temperatures near 39F with dew points in the upper 20s to 
low 30s; evaporative cooling at precipitation onset should 
support a transition to predominantly snow, though marginal 
surface temperatures will limit accumulation largely to unpaved 
surfaces. Farther north, 3 to 8 inches are expected at 
Washington Pass and along the North Cascades Highway, creating 
winter driving conditions. A trailing shortwave brings a 20 to 
40 percent chance of light precipitation across far northeast 
Washington and north Idaho Tuesday night. Snow levels will range
from 5000 to 5500 feet across the Columbia Basin, Palouse, and 
Spokane area, and 3500 to 4500 feet across northeast Washington 
and north Idaho.

Wednesday night through Thursday: An active synoptic pattern 
continues as a stronger frontal system approaches the Pacific 
Northwest Wednesday night into Thursday. Driven by a deeper 
southwesterly moisture plume and enhanced upper-level jet 
support, this system will penetrate farther inland. Early 
Thursday morning, low-level southeasterly warm advection into 
the east slopes of the Cascades will be sufficient to overcome 
the Cascade rain shadow, resulting in widespread precipitation 
across the Inland Northwest. Snow levels rise to 5000 to 6000 
feet overnight, resulting in lowland rain and moderate to heavy 
high elevation snow. The primary valley exception is the upper 
Methow Valley, where cold-air damming typically delays warming; 
model wet bulb profiles indicate precipitation will begin as 
heavy, wet snow before transitioning to rain or a rain/snow mix 
by late Thursday morning. National Blend of Models (NBM) 10th to
90th percentile snowfall ranges from 4.5 to 14.5 inches at 
Washington Pass and 1 to 4 inches at Sherman Pass. Those 
planning to travel over Washington Pass should be prepared for 
difficult driving conditions and winter driving conditions over 
Sherman Pass.

A trailing cold front moves eastward late Thursday morning 
through the afternoon, shifting precipitation into far eastern 
Washington and north Idaho while bringing an end to 
precipitation in central Washington. 25th to 75th percentile 
precipitation amounts indicates 0.10 to 0.50 inches in the 
Columbia Basin, 0.20 to 0.80 inches across the Okanogan Valley, 
far eastern Washington, and the north Idaho valleys, 0.40 to 1 
inch in the Idaho Panhandle mountains, and 1.50 to 2.50 inches 
in the Cascades. Winds will also increase with this front with 
southwest wind gusts up to 35 mph across the Columbia Basin, 
Palouse, and Spokane area. Showers persist along the Cascades 
behind the front, where weak instability (100 to 200 J/kg of 
SBCAPE) west of the Cascades extending to the crest may support 
isolated convective showers and a 15 to 20 percent chance of 
lightning.

Friday through Sunday: For the weekend, ensembles are 
suggesting a split flow pattern to develop over the northeast 
Pacific with an upper- level ridge in the Gulf of Alaska 
deflecting the polar jet northward, and an upper-level ridge 
building over the southwest with the subtropical jet directed 
into California. At this time, there is too much uncertainty in 
the synoptic pattern and track of systems Friday night into 
Saturday and then again on Sunday to speak to specific details. 
The current forecast carries a 20-60% of precipitation Friday 
through Sunday, reflecting this uncertainty. /vmt
